title: Why Your Input Tax Credit Doesn't Match GSTR-2B — and How to Fix It
seoTitle: ITC Not Matching GSTR-2B? How to Fix It in 2026
metaDescription: Your purchase register says one number and GSTR-2B says another. Here are the five real causes, a monthly reconciliation routine, and when to hand it over.
excerpt: Your purchase register says one number and the portal's drafted credit statement says another. The gap is normal; treating it as a quarterly surprise is what costs money. Here are the five real causes, a short monthly routine, and when to outsource it.

faq.question: Can I claim input tax credit that is missing from GSTR-2B?
faq.answer: Not safely. Until the supplier reports the invoice, the credit is not treated as available to you, and the portal is moving towards refusing a typed-over figure altogether. Chase the supplier in the same month rather than claiming and hoping to reconcile later. This is general information, not tax advice.

faq.question: What is the Invoice Management System in GST?
faq.answer: It is a portal facility where a buyer accepts, rejects or holds each inward invoice a supplier has reported, before the period's credit statement is drawn up. Taking no action counts as acceptance, so an unreviewed invoice still flows through.

faq.question: How often should a small business reconcile purchases against GSTR-2B?
faq.answer: Monthly, without exception. Four of the five common causes of a mismatch are fixable in the month they occur and nearly unfixable a year later, so the frequency matters more than the thoroughness.

faq.question: Is GSTR-3B still editable?
faq.answer: Not the liability half of it. Figures drawn from your outward return became fixed in the summary return from the July 2025 period onward, and any correction has to go through the same-period amendment return. A comparable lock on the credit side has been signalled but dates have moved, so check the portal's current advisories before planning around one.

faq.question: What happens if I do not pay a supplier within the prescribed period?
faq.answer: Credit taken on an invoice you have not settled within the window must be reversed, and can generally be reclaimed once payment is made. The mechanics and timing are worth confirming with your CA against your own facts.

bodyHtml:
Almost every small business in India has had the same month. You add up the GST on your purchase bills, you open the credit statement the portal has drafted for you, and the two numbers are not the same. Sometimes it is a few hundred rupees. Sometimes it is a supplier's entire quarter. Either way the return is due, and you have to decide what to claim before you have finished understanding why the gap exists.

The gap is normal. What is not normal, and what quietly costs money, is treating it as a once-a-quarter surprise instead of a monthly routine. This piece is about where the mismatch actually comes from, what has changed in the way the portal handles it, and the reconciliation habit that turns a panic into fifteen minutes of work.

This is general information, not tax advice. Rules and dates change, and your facts matter. Confirm anything here with your CA before you act on it.

Where the mismatch actually comes from

There are only a handful of real causes, and knowing which one you are looking at tells you what to do next.

  • The supplier has not filed yet. Your credit appears only once they report the invoice. A supplier who files quarterly will always be behind a monthly filer, and that is a timing difference rather than a loss.
  • The supplier filed it wrong. Wrong GSTIN, wrong invoice number, wrong period, or reported as business-to-consumer when it was business-to-business. The credit exists somewhere; it is just not pointed at you.
  • You booked it in a different month. The goods arrived on the 2nd, the bill is dated the 28th of the previous month, and your register and the statement are describing the same transaction in two different periods.
  • It was never eligible. Blocked credits, personal expenses run through the business, and the reverse charge cases people forget to treat separately.
  • You paid, or did not pay, within the window. Credit taken on an invoice you have not settled within the prescribed period has to be reversed and can be reclaimed once you pay.

Four of those five are fixable in the month they happen and nearly unfixable a year later. That is the whole argument for a monthly routine.

What has changed in how the portal handles this

Two things have shifted, and they push in the same direction: the portal increasingly decides your numbers rather than accepting them.

The first is the Invoice Management System, the portal facility that lets a buyer act on each inward invoice a supplier has reported — accept it, reject it, or hold it as pending — before the credit statement for the period is drawn up. Doing nothing counts as acceptance. That sounds like a small administrative addition and is not: it moves the first review of supplier data from your accountant's spreadsheet to the portal, on the portal's clock, and it gives a rejected invoice a formal route back to the supplier.

The second is the tightening of what you can type into the summary return. Auto-populated outward liability stopped being editable from the July 2025 period, with corrections routed through the amendment return for the same period instead. The equivalent lock on the credit side — that is, the input tax credit table matching the drafted statement and no longer accepting a typed-over figure — has been signalled as the next step, and various dates have circulated for it. Treat the direction as settled and the date as not. Check the current position on the portal's own advisories, or with your CA, before you plan around a specific month.

The practical consequence is the same either way. A year ago a mismatch was something you could claim through and reconcile later. Increasingly it is something you resolve before you file, or you do not claim it.

The monthly routine that prevents it

This takes about fifteen minutes once it is a habit, and most of that is the first step.

Keep the purchase side written down as it happens. Every inward bill goes into a Purchase Register on the day it arrives, with supplier GSTIN, invoice number, date, taxable value and tax split. Not at month end from a pile of paper. The register is what you reconcile against, and a register assembled in one sitting from memory inherits every error the pile already had.

Pull the statement and match on invoice number, not on totals. Totals hide two errors that cancel each other out. Matching line by line finds them. Anything in your register that is not in the statement goes on one list; anything in the statement that is not in your register goes on another.

Work the two lists differently. Missing-from-statement is a supplier problem and needs a message this week. Missing-from-register is usually your own bookkeeping — a bill that never got entered, which often means an expense you have not accounted for either.

Act on the invoices in the portal facility rather than letting the clock do it for you. Rejecting a genuinely wrong invoice is more useful than accepting it and arguing later, because the rejection is visible to the supplier.

Keep a supplier scorecard. A short note in your Supplier Book of who reports late, every month, is worth more at your next price negotiation than any reminder email. Chronic non-reporting is a real cost and belongs in the price you agree.

A worked example

Say a month's purchase register shows ₹4,10,000 of tax across eleven bills, and the drafted statement shows ₹3,52,000. The ₹58,000 gap is not one problem.

What you findTax involvedWhat to do
Quarterly-filing supplier, invoice not yet reported₹31,000Timing. It should appear next quarter — track it, do not chase it.
Supplier reported your GSTIN with one wrong digit₹18,000Message today. They amend it; the credit follows.
Bill dated the 29th, entered by you in the next month₹6,500Your cut-off. Fix the entry, not the claim.
Credit on an expense that was never eligible₹2,500Do not claim it. Reclassify the expense.

Four causes, four different actions, and only one of them is anybody else's fault. That is the usual shape of it. The business that does this monthly recovers the ₹18,000 in a week; the business that finds it at year end is asking a supplier to amend a return from three quarters ago, which is a conversation that rarely ends well.

When the supplier will not fix it

Some will not. The credit is genuinely yours, the invoice is genuine, and the supplier has stopped filing or stopped answering. You have three levers, in order of how much goodwill they cost.

Hold the payment. An unpaid balance is the only reliable reason a non-responsive supplier becomes responsive, and your Accounts Payable Aging tells you which balances are large enough to matter. Second, put the amount in writing with the invoice details and a date, so there is a record of the request rather than a memory of a phone call. Third, price it in: a supplier whose credit you routinely cannot claim is charging you more than their quotation says, and a vendor comparison that adds the unrecovered tax to their price often reorders the list.

When you are recalculating what a supply actually cost you once credit is not coming, the GST Calculator separates the tax from the base quickly enough to do it on the phone while you negotiate.

When to hand this to someone else

Reconciliation is one of the few bookkeeping jobs where outsourcing pays for itself in a way you can actually measure: the credit recovered against the fee. It is worth handing over when your purchase volume has passed the point where line-by-line matching takes a working day, when you have more than one GSTIN, when you have several months of unreconciled history to clear before you can start a clean routine, or when nobody in the business is doing it consistently and the gap has become something everyone avoids looking at.

That backlog case is the common one, and it is the one our bookkeeping and compliance service is built for — clean up the history, set the monthly routine, then hand it back or keep running it. The related habit on the money side is covered in our bank reconciliation checklist; the two together are most of what makes a set of books trustworthy.
